Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Massachusetts sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, challenging the constitutionality of a federal law that defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The state of Massachusetts says the Defense of Marriage Act denies same-sex couples essential rights. "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents," Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon. "Massachusetts has a single category of married persons, and we view all married persons equally and identically," she said. "DOMA divides that category into two distinct and unequal classes of marriage." The lawsuit argues that the act, which became law in 1996, denies same-sex couples essential rights and protections, including federal income tax credits, employment and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage and Social Security payments. "In enacting DOMA, Congress overstepped its authority, undermined states' efforts to recognize marriages between same-sex couples, and codified an animus towards gay and lesbian people," the state wrote in the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court. Massachusetts, the first state to legalize gay marriage, said that about 16,000 same-sex couples have been married there since 2004, when it began issuing marriage licenses. Since that time, the lawsuit said, "the security and stability of families has been strengthened in important ways throughout the state. " The state is challenging Section 3 of the law, which defines marriage as "a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife" and a spouse as "a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." Before the act, the lawsuit argues, defining marital status was the prerogative of the states. The law "eviscerated more than 200 years of federal government deference to the states with respect to defining marriage," it said. The lawsuit also argues that the law forces Massachusetts to treat same-sex married couples differently from heterosexual married couples, particularly through determining who qualifies for the state's Medicaid program, known as MassHealth, and whether a same-sex spouse of a veteran can be buried in a veteran cemetery. "But for DOMA, married individuals in same-sex relationships in the commonwealth would receive the same status, obligations, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married individuals in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal laws," the lawsuit said. The defendants named in the lawsuit include the Department of Health and Human Services, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki and the United States itself. Charles Miller, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, said the department will review the case but noted that President Obama supports the legislative repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act. In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders -- the same Boston-based group that successfully argued in 2003 for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts -- also sued the federal government over Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act. Besides Massachusetts, three other states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire will join their company when same-sex marriages become legal later this year and early next year.

counterfactuals.output:
# Massachusetts sues federal government over Defense of Marriage Act

**Boston, Massachusetts (CNN) —** Massachusetts filed a federal lawsuit Wednesday challenging the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act, arguing that the law forces the state to discriminate against legally married same-sex couples.

The lawsuit, filed by state Attorney General Martha Coakley in federal court in Boston, targets Section 3 of the 1996 law, which defines marriage for federal purposes as a union between one man and one woman.

Massachusetts became the first state to legalize same-sex marriage in 2004. State officials say the federal definition conflicts with Massachusetts law and prevents married same-sex couples from receiving the same federal benefits available to heterosexual couples.

The complaint argues that the federal law intrudes on an area traditionally regulated by the states and violates constitutional guarantees of equal protection. It also says Massachusetts risks losing federal funding if it treats same-sex spouses as married in programs administered jointly with the federal government.

Among the areas affected are Medicaid, veterans’ cemeteries and federal tax rules, according to the lawsuit. Because the federal government does not recognize same-sex marriages, state agencies must sometimes treat couples as married under Massachusetts law but unmarried under federal law.

Supporters of the Defense of Marriage Act say it preserves the traditional definition of marriage and allows the federal government to apply a uniform standard nationwide. The law also permits states to decline to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere.

The Obama administration has said the president supports repealing the law but, until Congress acts or a court overturns it, the Justice Department generally has a duty to defend federal statutes.

The Massachusetts case is separate from lawsuits brought by same-sex couples seeking federal recognition of their marriages. By filing as a state, Massachusetts is emphasizing both the rights of its residents and its authority to define marriage within its borders.

The lawsuit asks the court to declare Section 3 unconstitutional and prevent the federal government from applying it to Massachusetts and its legally married same-sex couples.

### Massachusetts challenge to DOMA Section 3

On July 8, 2009, Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley filed **_Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services_** in federal district court in Boston. It was the first lawsuit by a state challenging **Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA)**.

Section 3 defined “marriage” and “spouse,” for all federal purposes, as limited to opposite-sex couples. Massachusetts had legally recognized same-sex marriages since 2004, but DOMA required the federal government—and, in some federally funded programs, the Commonwealth itself—to disregard those marriages.

#### State-sovereignty argument

Massachusetts argued that Section 3:

- Intruded into the traditional and sovereign authority of states to determine marital status.
- Forced Massachusetts to treat some legally married couples as unmarried when administering federal-state programs.
- Required the Commonwealth either to discriminate against its own citizens or risk losing federal funding.
- Violated the **Tenth Amendment** and exceeded Congress’s authority under the **Spending Clause**.

The complaint also argued that the federal government lacked a sufficient justification for treating Massachusetts’s married same-sex couples differently, contrary to equal-protection principles incorporated in the Fifth Amendment.

#### Federal rights and benefits denied

Because DOMA refused to recognize valid same-sex marriages, affected couples could be denied or treated unequally regarding numerous federal protections, including:

- Joint federal income-tax treatment and other tax benefits.
- Social Security spousal and survivor benefits.
- Federal employee health, pension, and survivor benefits.
- Veterans’ spousal benefits and burial rights.
- Protections under federal health and Medicaid-related programs.
- Immigration sponsorship and other benefits tied to federal marital status.

The Massachusetts complaint emphasized concrete effects on state programs, including Medicaid administration, taxation of employee benefits, and eligibility for burial in federally supported veterans’ cemeteries.

#### Defendants

The complaint named:

- The **United States Department of Health and Human Services**.
- **Kathleen Sebelius**, then secretary of HHS, in her official capacity.
- The **United States Department of Veterans Affairs**.
- **Eric K. Shinseki**, then secretary of Veterans Affairs, in his official capacity.
- The **United States of America**.

In 2010, U.S. District Judge Joseph Tauro ruled Section 3 unconstitutional in the Massachusetts case. The issue ultimately reached the Supreme Court through a separate case, **_United States v. Windsor_**, which invalidated DOMA Section 3 in 2013.

# Federal Judge Backs Massachusetts Challenge to Defense of Marriage Act

**BOSTON, July 8, 2010 —** A federal judge ruled Thursday that the Defense of Marriage Act unconstitutionally interferes with Massachusetts’ authority over marriage, accepting the state’s argument that the federal law forces it to treat legally married same-sex couples differently from married opposite-sex couples.

U.S. District Judge Joseph L. Tauro found that Section 3 of the 1996 law, commonly known as DOMA, intrudes on an area traditionally regulated by the states and puts Massachusetts in an unlawful bind: discriminate against some couples whom the state recognizes as married, or risk losing federal money and violating federal program rules.

Massachusetts became the first state to legalize same-sex marriage in 2004. Under state law, marriages between two men or two women carry the same legal status as marriages between a man and a woman. But DOMA defines “marriage” for all federal purposes as the union of one man and one woman and defines “spouse” as a person of the opposite sex.

That conflict, Massachusetts argued, effectively creates two classes of married residents.

“The federal government cannot require Massachusetts to disregard its own marriage laws when administering programs jointly funded or regulated by Washington,” the state contended in its lawsuit.

## State says DOMA imposes unequal treatment

The case focuses on how the federal definition affects state-run programs, rather than only on whether individual couples are denied federal benefits.

Massachusetts said DOMA requires state officials to ignore otherwise valid marriages when applying federal standards involving health care, taxation and veterans’ services. Among the examples cited by the state:

- **Medicaid and other health programs:** Massachusetts may recognize a same-sex couple as married under state law, but federal rules implementing DOMA can require the state to treat the spouses as unmarried when determining eligibility or administering federally supported benefits.
- **Veterans’ cemeteries:** State officials argued that federal funding requirements could prevent Massachusetts from allowing a same-sex spouse to be buried with a veteran in a state veterans’ cemetery, even though state law recognizes the couple’s marriage.
- **State taxes and administration:** Because Massachusetts tax law relies in part on federal tax classifications, the state must create special procedures for same-sex married couples who are considered married by Massachusetts but unmarried by the federal government.
- **Employment and benefits systems:** State agencies may have to maintain separate rules or records because federal law refuses to recognize marriages the state considers fully valid.

The result, the state said, is not simply that the federal government withholds its own benefits. DOMA pressures Massachusetts itself to participate in differential treatment.

## A choice between discrimination and federal funds

Massachusetts framed the law as an unconstitutional condition on federal funding. Congress may attach requirements to money provided to states, but those requirements must be related to the federal program and cannot improperly coerce a state or compel it to violate constitutional guarantees, the state argued.

Under DOMA, Massachusetts said it must either administer certain programs using the federal government’s opposite-sex-only definition of marriage or risk losing federal support.

That requirement infringes on state sovereignty, according to the lawsuit, because marriage and domestic relations have historically been governed primarily by state law. Massachusetts decides who may marry within its borders, the state argued, and the federal government generally accepts those determinations when applying federal laws.

Tauro agreed that DOMA departed from that long-standing arrangement.

“The federal government, by enacting and enforcing DOMA, plainly encroaches upon the firmly entrenched province of the state,” the judge wrote.

## Equal marriages under state law, unequal treatment under federal rules

Massachusetts also argued that DOMA undermines the equality built into its marriage laws. Once the state chose to allow same-sex couples to marry, it assumed a duty to administer those marriages on equal terms.

Federal law, however, tells the state that some marriage certificates count for federal purposes and others do not, even when all were issued under the same Massachusetts statutes.

For example, an opposite-sex spouse and a same-sex spouse may have identical rights under state inheritance, family and property laws. Yet when the state administers a federally connected program, DOMA may require officials to recognize only the opposite-sex spouse.

That division, Massachusetts said, forces the Commonwealth to “identify and treat differently” a group of residents whom its own constitution and laws require it to treat equally.

## Federal government defends Congress’ authority

The Obama administration defended the statute in court, despite President Barack Obama’s stated opposition to DOMA and support for its repeal.

Justice Department lawyers argued that Congress has authority to define terms used in federal statutes and programs. They maintained that DOMA does not invalidate same-sex marriages under Massachusetts law; instead, it establishes a uniform federal definition for distributing federal benefits and obligations.

Supporters of DOMA have also argued that the law preserves consistency among federal programs while states adopt differing marriage policies.

Massachusetts rejected that reasoning, saying the federal government historically relied on state marital status even though state marriage laws have never been completely uniform. The state contended that DOMA singled out same-sex marriages rather than creating genuine nationwide uniformity.

## Companion ruling addresses individual couples

Tauro issued a separate decision Thursday in a related case brought by married same-sex couples and surviving spouses. In that case, the judge ruled that DOMA’s federal definition violates the equal-protection principles contained in the Fifth Amendment.

Together, the decisions strike at the core of Section 3, which affects hundreds of federal laws and programs involving taxes, Social Security, immigration, pensions, health insurance and survivor benefits.

The rulings do not immediately erase DOMA nationwide. The federal government can appeal, and the dispute is likely to move through higher courts.

For Massachusetts, however, the central claim is now backed by a federal trial judge: The federal government may not recognize the Commonwealth’s marriage licenses for some purposes while compelling the state to treat one group of legally married couples as if they were unmarried.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

In July 2009, Massachusetts sued the federal government in **Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**, challenging Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which defined marriage for federal purposes as only between a man and a woman.

Massachusetts argued that DOMA forced the state to disregard marriages that were valid under state law. This created conflicts in programs such as **MassHealth**, where the state had to treat married same-sex couples as unmarried when administering federally funded Medicaid benefits or risk losing federal funds. DOMA also interfered with **veterans’ burial rights**: Massachusetts allowed same-sex spouses to be buried together in state veterans’ cemeteries, but federal funding rules did not recognize those spouses and potentially jeopardized cemetery grants. More broadly, legally married same-sex couples were denied federal benefits and protections available to different-sex spouses, including tax, health, retirement, and survivor benefits.

The suit emphasized Massachusetts’s authority over domestic relations. In **Goodridge v. Department of Public Health** in 2003, the state’s highest court ruled that excluding same-sex couples from marriage violated the Massachusetts Constitution; same-sex marriages began there on **May 17, 2004**, making Massachusetts the first U.S. state to permit them.

A federal district court ruled DOMA’s Section 3 unconstitutional in 2010, and the First Circuit affirmed in 2012. The Supreme Court later invalidated Section 3 nationwide in **United States v. Windsor** in 2013.

# Massachusetts challenges federal marriage law

**BOSTON, July 8, 2009** — Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley filed a federal lawsuit Wednesday challenging part of the Defense of Marriage Act, arguing that the 1996 law forces the state to discriminate against legally married same-sex couples.

“The Defense of Marriage Act forces Massachusetts to discriminate against its own citizens,” Coakley said in announcing the lawsuit. “This is a violation of the United States Constitution and should not be allowed to continue.”

The complaint, filed in U.S. District Court in Boston, targets Section 3 of DOMA, which defines marriage for federal purposes as the union of one man and one woman. Massachusetts argues that the provision denies federal recognition to marriages that are valid under state law and interferes with the state’s administration of programs involving Medicaid, veterans’ cemeteries and other federally funded services.

Coakley said the federal government should not be able to require Massachusetts to treat one group of married residents differently from another. The lawsuit contends that DOMA exceeds federal authority, intrudes on the state’s traditional power to regulate marriage and places unconstitutional conditions on federal funding.

Massachusetts became the first state to allow same-sex couples to marry after the state’s highest court ruled in 2003 that excluding them from civil marriage violated the Massachusetts Constitution. Marriages began in May 2004.

The state’s case is distinct from a separate lawsuit filed earlier in 2009 by Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders on behalf of same-sex couples and surviving spouses. That case, *Gill v. Office of Personnel Management*, argues that DOMA violates constitutional equal-protection guarantees by withholding federal benefits available to opposite-sex married couples.

By the time Massachusetts filed its challenge, same-sex marriage was also legal in Connecticut and Iowa. Vermont had enacted a law scheduled to take effect later in 2009, while New Hampshire had approved one for 2010. Maine lawmakers had also passed a same-sex marriage law, though opponents were seeking to overturn it through a statewide referendum. California recognized thousands of same-sex marriages performed before voters approved Proposition 8 in November 2008.

DOMA also contains a separate provision allowing states to decline to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere. Massachusetts’ lawsuit focuses on the federal definition of marriage rather than that state-recognition provision.
